The PRESIDENTIAL Platforms and Candidates for 1856.—No. 1,


Not since the memorable canvass of 1850 has there occurred more important political contest than the present. The unusual spectacle is presented of three PRESIDENTIAL candidates in the field leading three great parties of the country. We propose to consider briefly their character and claims and to analyze the platforms on which they respectively stand. The present contest is not merely struggle for the distribution of patronage, not merely attempt to settle the ordinary issues of party but is actual war between those who desire to preserve the Federal Constitution in its purity, as it came from Washington and from Madison, and those who pervert it and who seek its essential alteration or destruction.


We have at last that which Washington so much deprecated, a great geographical party. The Abolition party which voted for Birney in 1854 was a small one, and did not cause much apprehension. In 1848 when it supported Van Buren, standing the Buffalo platform, it had much increased, and during the present administration it, stimulated by liberal participation in public patronage and by the repeal of the Missouri Compromise, has so strengthened as to weld a fearful power.


Under the name of the Republican party (called more properly in the South Black Republican) it has frustrated the Democratic party in nearly every Northern State; it has, especially in the last few months, been drawing to its ranks so many leading Democrats that the only safe and polite course is to raise the barrier of Americanism against this hideous sectional party, and for all who hold national and constitutional views to unite in the American party, not merely by words but by glorious deeds done in the face of the country. The American party is of recent origin, scarcely more than two years old, but in that period it has grown with gigantic growth. The rapidity with which, like fire over prairie, it spread over the country is one of the marvels of the times. Houston, Clemens, Foote, Borland, and Donelson, with many other distinguished and undistinguished Democrats, pushed by the new party, saw in the new party means of restoring the government to its original purity and accomplishing actual reforms. They wisely preferred aiming at practical good to senseless lowering over questions like that of the currency and high protective tariff, which had been settled authority lively by the people,—aye, which were dead and buried.


No rejecting person, acquainted with the foreign element of the country, can deny that at the time of the organization of the American party, there was need of reform in the naturalization laws, and in their administration; that there need of reform in those States especially, which foolishly granted the foreigner suffrage before he had become citizen of the United States. The old parties were each or retain the ascendency. Offices, in undue proportion, were given to foreigners, bribes for the foreign vote. It is not strange that foreigners, coming as they do from countries where their privileges were few or none, and placed as many of them were soon after their arrival, over the sons of the soil, should become turbulent and insolent. When it was found that half a million of aliens had been cast upon our shores in one year, the year 1854, and that three millions had arrived in the ten years previous, that nearly all of them ignorant of our language and institutions, that many were paupers, many criminals fresh from the prisons of the Old World, it was felt by many that something must be done to remove or diminish the evil. The old parties had not the moral courage to do it. It was necessary, therefore, to form a new party for this and other forms.


The founders of the American party also perceived that the Catholics, as a sect acting in the politics of this country, it did not escape notice that John Hughes, the head of their Church in this country, and subject only to the Pope, moved as a unit, and whenever his party came into power he was enabled with liberal hand to dole out to his compliant subjects official patronage. The Catholic Church, it is true, is divided into Gallicans and Ultramontanes, the latter constituting the large majority, who hold that the Pope has temporal supremacy overriding all other allegiances and authorities. Brownson's Review, endorsed by nearly all the Catholic Bishops in the United States, and Freeman's Journal, the organ of Hughes, (both published in this country) advocated the Ultramontane doctrine. The American party did wisely therefore, in condemning in all their platforms this higher-law doctrine and in resolving to support one for office who held it. The 9th section of the National American platform says:


"No person should be selected for political station, whether of native or foreign BIRTH, who recognises any allegiance or obligation of any description to any foreign prince, potentate, or power, or who refuses to recognise the Federal and State constitutions (each within its sphere) as paramount to all other laws, as rules of political action."


Thus it appears our party wars against higher-law doctrines of every kind—the Constitution of the United States, when fairly interpreted, is doctrine high enough and good enough for us. We wage uncompromising war against Sewardites and against those who look to Rome and not to Washington for their temporal ruler and for their expounders of law. The hackneyed falsehood that the American party are opposed to religious freedom is scarcely worthy of serious refutation. The 10th section of its national platform of this year proclaims the principle that "there must be no interference with religious faith, or worship, and no tests of Office." Our party bitterly denounces and opposes everything in the least approaching union of Church and State, being unwilling that religion should rise and fall with the changes of party, or be subjected to the corrupting influences of such alliance. It will protect, not interfere, with any Catholic in his worship, no matter how superstitious, but it begs to be excused from having any part in making rulers of those who look to an authority beyond which they deem paramount to the fundamental laws of our land.


The Philadelphia platform of February 21st, 1856, is the one which Mr. Fillmore has accepted. It is briefer and clearer than party platforms usually are. It is, by far more consistent with itself than that of Cincinnati. The platform justly gives preference to natives over foreigners with respect to office. In the 9th section of the platform it is declared that there shall be no interference with the vested rights of foreigners. An intention to interfere was never fairly inferable from any proceeding of the party, but this cypress disclaimer is given to prevent possible Democratic misstatement in this respect. Twenty-one years residence for foreigners before being allowed suffrage is proposed as an amendment to our laws. That period is selected because natives have to wait that long. The foreigners who come to US are in a worse state than political infancy. They have not only to acquire new political ideas but unlearn old. Generally of the least desirable class, they come seeking not freedom but bread. Immigrant vessels have often seemed to my eyes floating pauper houses. Surely raw foreigners furnish not the material for intelligent voters, still less for American rulers.
